I just watched [John Oliver's latest video about debt buyers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hxUAntt1z2c). He talks about companies that buy overdue debt at a fraction of the owed sum. The main problem I have with his statements is that "sometimes" being in debt is not one's fault. And then if you can't pay it back, you're subject to the harassment of the mean debt collectors, sometimes with admittedly questionable methods.

I was always pretty sure that there is no way that you can be in debt without it being your fault. Debt doesn't just appear, you willingly have to sign a contract and take the money. Either because you're investing (house) or because you just live above your means (luxury car, smartphone, etc.). And if you can't repay it, it's because you made bad decisions in the number and/or amount of debts you have.

His example of being in debt without fault was a guy who had to get intensive care because of breathing problems. Then the insurance refused to pay, so the hospital charged them $80k. I find this hard to believe, because being in the ICU is pretty much always a catastrophic medical emergency. So even if you have the shittiest insurance out there, with just catastrophic coverage, how could being in the ICU not be covered? If they had no insurance and took the gamble of being able to pay the medical bills themselves, that would be easy and again their fault. But the insurance can't just be like, nah, we're not paying, tough luck. There has to be a contract stating what the coverage is. So how could it possibly happen that they had insurance, but didn't know it wouldn't cover the ICU?

So is his debt without fault statement legit or just his liberal propaganda against evil capitalist debt buyers and collectors that are harassing innocent people for not at all being in fault of overspending?
How can you be in debt without it being your fault?

It's legit. Insurance does not always cover 100% of the bill. This all depends on the deductible and co-pays. One might have, say, a 5000 dollar deductible but with a 10% hospital co-pay. If the bill is 100,000, you will need to fork up 15 grand. That is, of course, assuming you have insurance to begin with. If you don't have insurance, you just got a 100 grand bill. That's when you make a call to Chapter 7. (all of this is in the US).

If you don't have insurance or your insurance fails to pay your hospital/doctor bill, you really need to call said doctor/hospital & tell them that you will be paying out of pocket. Ask them if there is any way the bill can be reduced. Almost everytime, they will lower the charges significantly. Both because they want to be payed (even if it is a lesser amount) but also because insurance in the US is so messed up that it pays pre-determined amounts for things, even if said amount is higher than the hospital/doctor would otherwise charge.

Also, if times are tough, you can apply for financial hardship at many hospitals. They'll look at your income, basic bills (mortgage, student loans), and forgive a certain percentage, up to 99%, of the debt. They'll also lower the bill first to help you pay it.

Well, in the video they stated that the insurance covered nothing. While $15k is not nothing, it's a different league than their $80k. Most people pay more for a car than that. Also, insurance plans usually have an out-of-pocket maximum way less than $80k. In fact I just learned that there is a maximum of $6,850 for an individual and $13,700 for a family plan.

Again, if you don't have insurance and need medical care, yes, that's going to be expensive. But it was still your choice not to purchase an insurance (or apply for Medicaid, etc.) and hope for the best. But if you have coverage, there shouldn't be unexpected debt suddenly bankrupting you.

There were a couple of things your cousin could have done after paying the debt off, including contacting the FTC I believe. Debtors cannot legally buy debt that was paid off. He (all of us, really) have the power to negotiate debts after they've been bought as well.

Debts have a statute of limitations for being reported on credit reports, usually 7 years. You can still get bills for it, but the collectors cannot report it on your credit report after so many years. And, it's not so many years after you incurred the debt, it's 7 or so years after the last time you admitted to owing the debt and making a partial payment.

There are also certain procedures debt collectors have to go through, and any missteps allow the person who owes to threaten or pursue legal action against the debtors.
